beats.got: nothing new, it's a title.

beats.trigger: The filesystem is the meeting room.

beats.got: I'll end up with an answer on my own pricing question. That's the reason I'm here.

beats.trigger: Three agents search Confluence, OneDrive and practitioner articles, and three more decide what it means.
beats.got: The setup uses my real sources: wiki, docs and the internet. I'd be able to use that.

beats.trigger: Writing a file changes your folder. Slack changes another system.
beats.got: Posting to Slack is a different kind of action from writing a file, and it needs approval. Fine, but the demo is a toy and has nothing to do with pricing.

beats.trigger: Push back when the first answer restates the problem.
beats.got: The agent has to name the one obstacle behind my pricing pilot, and if it just restates my problem I should push it harder. That's useful.

beats.trigger: Three retrievers fetch raw material on your challenge into `sources/`; a fourth session curates it into `memory/`.
beats.got: Separate sessions pull wiki, docs and web into files, and a curator sorts them. The files are still there on Monday. Twenty-eight minutes is long, though, and I'd skip the internet retriever if I were short on time.

beats.trigger: You can't yet tell if the answer is right. That is expected. Name the doubt; don't fix it here.
beats.got: The answer comes out confident and I can't verify it yet. My CFO would ask about exactly that, so I'm glad it says so openly.

beats.trigger: Two ways to split an agent: three retrievers in separate windows, three stances inside one session.
beats.got: I just did both of these in the exercises, so this is a recap.

beats.trigger: Build one agent per recurring workflow: a single `.md` file, guardrailed for that job.
beats.got: One agent per repeating job, not one giant agent and not a hundred tiny ones.

beats.trigger: Default to one agent with a good prompt.
beats.got: The default is one agent, and splitting costs coordination. That's honest advice and I don't hear much of it.

beats.trigger: A backward planner and a reframer in the same voice are one agent pretending to be two.
beats.got: There are three tests for splitting: access, dialect and stance. I can check my own setup against them.

beats.trigger: Split for a reason, not because "three is more thorough".
beats.got: nothing new. It's the same point as 'start with don't', said again.

beats.trigger: The synthesizer then commits to one diagnosis and drops what does not serve it.
beats.got: Without a framework the synthesizer averages the views. A framework forces it to commit, so the output comes from the structure I give it and not from a cleverer prompt.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output? If yes, write that one prompt.
beats.got: nothing new. Third time I've read 'default to one agent'.

beats.trigger: Each helper gets one job, reports back as a file and disappears.
beats.got: Separate sessions for long-lived agents with their own tools. Helpers inside one session for quick parallel thinking.

beats.trigger: One agent can call another for a different stance, source zone, or working style.
beats.got: nothing new. It's the previous slide's distinction, now in more abstract wording.

beats.trigger: A retriever finds two numbers and the curator keeps one.
beats.got: Handoffs are where conflicting numbers disappear unnoticed. That's the kind of contradiction in my own sources I want caught.

beats.trigger: If one well-prompted agent does the job, write that prompt.
beats.got: nothing new. This is the fourth time it's been said.

beats.trigger: Agents get stuck: wrong source, three views averaged into mush, the wrong file written, confident right before a failed handoff.
beats.got: A list of the ways my setup will go wrong. Realistic.

beats.trigger: Prompt your stuck system to diagnose whether the bug lives in the sources, the processing, or the boundary between agents.
beats.got: Before fixing anything I ask the agent whether the problem is in the sources, the processing or the boundary.

beats.trigger: Write down the lesson: add a rule to CLAUDE.md: what to read first, what not to smooth over, which output format to produce, when to stop and ask.
beats.got: Each fix gets written into a rules file, so the next run starts smarter and a teammate could read it. That is what I need for my team.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the four prompts, the retrieval files, the synthesizer's briefing and the conversation, then rewrites CLAUDE.md in place and reports what changed.
beats.got: The agent audits its own handoffs and updates the rules file, and I push back where it's wrong. It's a useful five minutes.

beats.trigger: The audit reads how your agents handed work to each other. It does not check whether the briefing is true.
beats.got: The audit checks how the agents worked together, not whether the briefing is correct. That is exactly the gap my CFO would find.

beats.trigger: New evidence tests the memory's structure.
beats.got: An optional prompt to stress-test the memory folder after I add more sources. I'd probably run it before I rerun the brief.

take_homes: Default to one agent. Split only when the sources differ in access, dialect or stance.
Give the synthesizer a framework, such as Rumelt's kernel, so it commits to one diagnosis instead of averaging. This does more than a better prompt.
The files are the shared place: sources, memory and a rules file that records what went wrong. A teammate could pick them up. The briefing still isn't verified, and I need to check it myself.

monday.move: Rerun the crux and retriever setup on the usage-pricing pilot with fresh data, put the sources and memory folder somewhere shared, and ask the agent to flag where my sources disagree. Then send the briefing to the pricing working group with its open doubts labelled.
monday.who: Me first, then one or two people from my team of fourteen.
monday.when: Monday morning, about two hours, before the pricing working group meeting.
monday.stop_condition: If the synthesized briefing contradicts the Q2 review and I can't tell which is right, I stop and check the numbers by hand before it goes out.
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for the context files. Everyone keeps their own copy, and the course doesn't say where the folder should live.

misconception.why: I came in thinking the skill was writing better prompts. The framework slide and the files and rules in CLAUDE.md showed the output depending more on structure and shared files than on wording. Only 'shaken', because the prompts were still pasted in and did most of the visible work.

one_line: Good hands-on hour on my real problem, and honest that the answer isn't verified yet. The 'use one agent' point was made four times, and we were never shown how a team shares the folder.
